messages.subject: Adjusting raw point-count data
parts:
I have a motley collection of songbird point-count data from three cypres=
s=20
swamp habitat-types, some data with distance information, other data can=20=

only be reliably summarized as total number of detections within 50m. I=20=

would like to adjust these raw 50m count data with detection probabilitie=
s=20
from DISTANCE analyses from the same habitat-type. I'm in over my head=20=
with DISTANCE, so I'm hoping someone might point out errors in the=20
following strategy.=20=20

Would it be appropriate to analyze the subset of the data with radial=20
distances either in the MCDS engine, using habitat-type as a factor=20

covariate, or the CDS engine post-stratified by habitat, then integrate=20=

the detection probability functions from 0-50m and, finally, divide the=20=

raw counts by the habitat-specific detection probability?=20=20

Would this yield a density estimate or an estimate of abundance? If it=20=

yields abundance, then I assume all data should be corrected in the same=20=

way for further analyses (AIC, CCA) relating abundance to habitat=20
variables?

Only about 1/3 of the species in the community have sufficient detections=
=20
to model the global detection function, which complicates any analyses to=

=20
describe the effects of habitat variables on the community. Any=20
suggestions?

For those who may have questions about adjusting raw count data, I've=20

copied a long collection of posts concerning this topic that I've found o=
n=20
the listserv , below. As an aside, I thought Dr. Thomas's reply to Nick=20=
Bickle on 5 Oct 2004 concerning general rules-of-thumb for DISTANCE=20

sampling was especially useful, concisely stated basic information. I=20=

think it should be printed on the overleaf of any subsequent editions of=20=

the Intro book. (By the way, does anyone else's Intro book smell like a=20=

chemical waste dump? I need to wash my hands every time I handle it.)


Apologies for my ignorance.
Hoping for a reply (without "RTFM!"),
Dave

Hi James,
> >Now, I wish to adjust my counts (number of detections within 100-m=20

radius) to account for variation in detection probability resulting from=20=

variation in shrub cover.

The easy way, assuming each point is entered as a sample in Distance, is=20=

to set up a new Model Definition and tick the box to estimate density by=20=

sample in the Estimate tab. If you want abundance by point, it's simply=20=

density*pi*w^2 where w is truncation distance.

However, if you want to calculate abundance in each sample (point) by=20
hand, you can use the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator: estimated=20

abundance =3D sum(1/estimated p_i) where the sum is over all animals coun=
ted=20
at the point, and p_i is the estimated probability of detecting the ith=20=

animal, given it is within the truncation distance. To calculate p_i, se=
e=20
the Distance online help -- look in the index under Detection function,=20=
formulae, about. Note that if you don't have animal level covariates=20

(which it appears you don't) then p_i will be the same for all animals at=
=20
a point, so the above reduces to estimated abundance =3D n/p where n i=
s=20
the count at the point and p is the estimated probability of detecting an=

=20
animal given it is within the truncation distance.

As an aside, assuming that your stands vary in size, then by locating one=
=20
point in each stand you have a design with a different proportion of the=20=

stand area surveyed in each point (different "coverage probability" in=20=

each stand). If you're also interested in calculating an average density=

=20
over all stands, you'll need to take this into account. You could=20
calculate a weighted mean of the stand densities, with the weight being=20=

the proportion of the stand area surveyed.

Hope this helps,

- Len

Hi James,

I don't think you need to do anything by hand, unless you're a=20

masochist! I wasn't 100% clear in my previous message so I'll try to=20=

lay it out better here. For that reason I'm also cc'ing this to the list=

,=20
in case anyone else wants to do the same thing.

I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but=20=

with habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the=

=20
probability of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the=20

point and that the animal is present within the truncation distance. You=
=20
then want to calculate density (or abundance) at each point using this=20=

habitat-specific probability of detection.

You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the Model=
=20
Definition | Estimate tab. Under "Quantities to estimate and level of=20=

resolution", for the Density and the detection function rows, tick both=20=
the "Global" and "Sample" columns. Make sure you have habitat as a=20
covariate. For more about this, see the online help, Chapter 9, Defining=

=20
MCDS models, Estimating the detection function at multiple levels.

The output you will get will be density for each point, and p_i for=20

animals at each point too. (You will also get abundance for each point,=20=

but there's a bug in Distance where the area used to calculate this is=20=
currently wrong so it's acutally abundance for the whole study area=20
assuming density at that point applies to the whole study area -- this bu=

g=20
is fixed in the next version of Distance to be released.)

You *can* calculate probability of detection by hand if you really want=20=

to =96 but it's going to require some work. We want p_i, the probability=
of=20
detecting an animal at each point, given that it is within the truncation=
=20
distance. Note, this isn't the probability of detecting the animal at=20=

it's observed distance -- it's the probability given that the animal was=20=

somewhere between 0 and w. We could use the observed distances but then=20=
estimation tends to be less reliable -- for more on this see the MCDS=20
chapter of the up-coming Advanced Distance Sampling book. Because we're=20=
integrating out the distance component, the only covariate left is=20

habitat, so that means the p_i's will be the same for all animals at each=
=20
point, given the amount of shrub cover. So what you need to do is progra=
m=20
Excel (or something better) to work out probability of detection for a=20=

given covariate level and distance, and then program Excel (or whatever)=20=

to integrate this function between 0 and w, using numerical integration=20=

such as Simpson's rule. As you can see, it's probably easier to let=20
Distance do it!
Specific replies to your questions about estimating p below, should you=20=

still
want to do it.

Cheers,

- Len

On Thu, 13 May 2004 14:58:43 -0400, Tucker, James wrote:

> >Dr. Thomas:
> >

> >Thank you for replying to my question. I tried to estimate density by=20=

sample, but I do not have enough observations for most samples (points) t=
o=20
estimate probability of detection for individual points. Could you pleas=

e=20
help me with the following questions?
> >If I calculate p_i, the estimated probability of detecting the ith=20

animal, will the mean for the p_i at a point be a good estimate for=20
probability of detection at that point?

As I explained above, you could do it this way, but better to use the=20
definition I gave of p_i as probability of detection given the animal is=20=
between 0 and w, rather than probability at a given distance. In the=20
former case, all p_i's for each animal at a point are the same (because=20=
you have no animal level covariates other than distance).
> >I do not have animal level covariates, but I want to adjust p_i to=20
account for the influence of shrub cover at each point. Does the=20
calculation of "s" in the equation below include measurements for shrub=20=

cover at the individual points?

Yes.

> >Effort : 86.00000
> > # samples : 86
> > Width : 100.0000
> > # observations: 297
> > Model
> > Hazard Rate key, k(y) =3D 1 - Exp(-(y/s)**-A(2))
> > s =3D A(1) * Exp(fcn(A(3)))
> > Parameter A(1) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
> > Parameter A(2) is the power parameter.
> > Parameter A(3) is the coefficient of covariate ARCSHRUB.
> > Point Standard Percent Coef. 95 Percent
> > Parameter Estimate Error of Variation Confidence Interv=
> >In the above equation for "s", what is "fcn"? I plan to use an Excel=20=
spreadsheet to do the calculations. I am somewhat mathematically=20
challenged, so it would be great if you know Excel and can tell me the=20=

function in Excel that corresponds to "fcn".

Fcn is short for function. It's a bit obscure I agree. Your shrub=20
covariate is a non-factor covariate - let's denote it's value at a=20
particular point as z. Then to evaluate Exp(fcn(A(3))), you calculate Ex=

p
(z*A(3)). So, overall: k(y)=3D 1 - Exp(-(y/[A(1)*exp(z*A(3))])**-A(2))
> >In the following equation for probability of detection, g(y)=3Dkey(y)

[1+series (y)]/key(0)[1+series(0)] what parameters do I use to calculate=20=

series(y)? The example in Distance/Help uses A(3), but that example does=

=20
not include a covariate.

You didn't have any series expansion terms in your model, judging from=20=

your output above. In this case k(0)=3D1, so you don't need the bottom l=
ine=20
so k(y)=3Dg (y).

As an aside, the above parameter estimates appear to indicate that there=20=

is very little effect of the habitat covariate (A(3), unless your habitat=
=20
values are very large numbers. For example, if z=3D1x10^11, then exp(z*A=
(3)) is 1.00926. Did AIC really select this model over one with no=20

covariates? Also, the values of A(1) and A(2) seem to indicate a wide=20=

shoulder and then a steep drop off -- although "wide" is relative to the=20=

scale of your measurements.

Hope this helps,

- Len

Hi Nick, list,

What you're proposing is what we sometimes call "spatial modeling"=20

or "spatial density surface estimation". I'll attempt an answer, but I'm=
=20
no expert so others may want to contribute more. Also, there's some stuf=

f=20
on this in Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.

To begin with, you need to do the detection function modeling in=20
Distance. You could either stratify by habitat, or put habitat in as a=20=
factor covariate in the MCDS engine. If you have enough data, and no=20

problems such as avoidance, rounding, etc, then you could try both and le=
t=20
AIC tell you which is better. If using MCDS then you could include other=
=20
covariates too. Once you've finished this modeling, you want an estimate=

=20
of detection probability by point (p_k) (Note, I'm omitting hats from=20

estimates to avoid cumbersome text notation. Also, for now, I'm assuming=
=20
you don't have any species level covariates such as cluster size). To do=
=20
this, you ask for density by sample, as in my reply to "Adjusting counts=

=20
for delectability and covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004).
Now you need to incorporate the estimates of p_k into the spatial model=20=
for the bird counts. To my knowledge there are three ways to do this:
1. Divide the observed count at each point n_k by the estimated p_k to ge=

t=20
an estimate of abundance at each point N_k. This abundance is non-
integer, so:
2. you might want to divide N_k by the area of each point (pi*w^2) to get=

=20
an estimated density at each point D_k. Doesn't make much difference=20
really. Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson error=20=
term as the response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?=20

3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use=20=

pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius for=20=

that point.

Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the=20
counts. However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level=20

covariates, such as sex of bird or cluster size. In that case, you don't=
=20
know what the effective detection radius is when you observe no birds --=20=

but you do know that the estimate of density is 0. If you have species=20=

level covariates in 1 or 2 you estimate N_k by the sum of 1/p_i for each=20=

bird i detected at the point. There is a section of the online manual=20=

that says how to calculate p_i for each animal given the parameter=20
estimates of the detection function.

In practice, two problems usually present themselves:

1. Overdispersion. Often many points have 0 birds seen, so you get data=20=

with lots of zeros and relatively few high counts (or high D_ks if the=20=

p_ks are sometimes small). Can be hard to model. Can perhaps investigat=

e=20
the various zero-inflated models that are out there?

2. Variance estimation. How does one incorporate the variance due to=20

estimating the detection function in the final variance estimate from the=
=20
spatial model? An easy way is a nonparametric bootstrap or jackknife of=20=

points, but you need plenty of points for this. Various parametric=20
bootstraps have been proposed - I think there is something on this in=20
Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book. It may be possible to=20=
do something analytic based on the delta method -- don't know.
So, hope this helps -- as I said others may be able to contribute more.=20=

I'll answer your second question in a separate email.

Cheers,

- Len

Hi Nick, list,
> >Second question (sorry, its very basic compared to the first).

> >I currently work in conservation in Indonesia and I regularly see=20
> >DISTANCE used as a simple recipe for calculating absolute densities,
> >typically using all default values in the programme (against all

> >advice!), and without any great understanding of what AICs, CVs, CIs etc=

> >actually mean.
Argh! Hopefully you can do your bit in training people to make=20
intelligent use of the program. Also, I've found in general that people=20=
who have a poor understanding of the program options also have a poor=20
understanding of how to design surveys and implement field methods that=20=
give reliable results. Just my prejudice I guess.
> >Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated
> >density but this is regularly justified by saying that "the 'real' value=
> >must be within the confidence intervals somewhere". What is the simple
> >answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will=

> >give you little information on density, or that a CV of over 20%
> >suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
> >already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
> >My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
> >density estimate outright?

I'm afraid it's not that simple. Getting a reliable estimate requires=20=

more than just an "adequate" sample size of observations, and the require=
d=20
sample size depends on factors such as the type of survey (points require=

=20
more than lines), and shape of the detection function (wide shoulders=20
require fewer observations to accurately model). Also, remember that you=

=20
also need a "decent" sample size of lines or points for reliable=20
estimation of the encounter rate variance.

Here's a very rough checklist for initial assessment of a study:

- were the lines/points laid out according to a randomized survey design?=
=20=20
Ideally there should be 20 or more lines or points - many fewer than that=
=20
and I'd doubt the encounter rate variance estimates. If the analysis is=20=

stratified, you'd like 20 lines per stratum if possible.

- is g(0) likely to be 1?

- is animal movement likely to be a problem? (is there evasive movement,=20=

or do animals move at more than 1/3-half the speed of the observer for=20=

line transects; were the point transects performed over a "long" time=20
period (ie not a snapshot)

- were distances measured accurately?

- does the detection function have a wide shoulder?

- is the sample size of observations reasonable? (60-80 recommended,=20
although for wide shoulders and line transects can get away with far=20
fewer). If the detection function is estimated by stratum, you'd like 60-=

80 observations by stratum if possible.

- does the analysis look like it was performed competently?

- do the reported results give both the estimate and CI/CV, and=20
interpretation of the results take account of the uncertainty in the=20
estimate.

I've probably forgotten something, but hope this helps. Perhaps someone=20=

else will be willing to stick their neck out and offer more absolute rule=

s=20
of thumb!

- Len

Hello list,
I'm hoping to get some feedback on my proposed method for adjusting raw=20=

abundance counts (a.k.a. relative abundance) with Distance-derived=20
probabilities of detection. I am doing a study of forest landbird=20
communities at 75 sites along an urbanization gradient. I conducted poin=

t=20
transects at these sites (5 stations per site, visited 3 times each),=20

placing detections into the following distance intervals: 0-25 m, 25-50 m=
,=20
50-75 m, and 75-100 m. I am happy to defend my use of intervals, but it'=
s=20
not really relevant here. Ultimately, I want to have site-specific count=

s=20
of all species that I can use as dependent variables in multiple=20
regressions and other analyses.

I wish to use program Distance to adjust the raw counts of birds. I=20

cannot do this on a site-by-site basis, except perhaps for all species=20=

combined, because of a low number of detections. (The total number of=20=

bird detections of all species per site across all visits to all stations=
=20
averaged about 314 birds.) I thought, however, that I could put sites=20=
into urbanization categories (strata) and calculate stratum-specific=20

probabilities of detection with which to adjust the raw counts (or more=20=

likely, the average count across 3 visits and 5 stations) at each site.=20=
=20
The use of separate detection functions for urbanization categories makes=

=20
sense to me, as noise levels, which often interfere with my mostly=20

auditory detections, increase with urbanization. So I placed the sites i=
n=20
6 categories of urbanization (low to high), calculated species-specific=20=

probabilities of detection for each category, and then adjusted counts of=
=20
each species at each site by dividing them by the probability of detectio=
n=20
for that site's category. I might use 3 urbanization categories for some=
=20
species if I don't have enough observations to get a reliable probability=
=20
of detection using 6 categories, and possibly use a global probability of=
=20
detection for species that still have too few observations. One potentia=

l=20
problem with this approach, if I understand correctly, is that the=20

estimates within a development class will not be independent because they=
=20
were derived from the same detection function. I don't know how much of =

a=20
problem this is.

I have done some preliminary analyses, with mixed results. It seems=20
difficult to get a reliable detection function. There is rarely=20

a "shoulder," as I'm working with four intervals and the probability of=20=

detection nearly always drops off quickly after the first category. Still=
,=20
the goodness-of-fit tests and the CVs seem okay. Second, nearly all the=20=

probabilities of detection for the highest development category are in th=

e=20
neighborhood of 0.10 - 0.15. When I adjust the raw counts,

this yields abundance values that are 6x-10x the raw counts. Some of the=
=20
adjusted values seem way too high, based on years of experience counting=20=
birds in this area. Forty-five jays on average at a single point=20

transect? No way. Further, some of the probability of detection values=20=

are absurdly low. Finally, zero values are unadjusted by this method, bu=
t=20
zero values could actually represent undetected birds. Incidentally, I=20=

likely have similar problems to those discussed in mid-April on this=20
listserve: counting more than singing males, and problems with=20

the "snapshot" assumption.=20=20

I could use various types of advice. What do you think of this approach=20=

over all? Is there a better way? Essentially, how can one use Distance=20=

to calculate site-specific abundances when there are not enough detection=
s=20
at each site to model site-specific detection functions? Can I somehow=20=

use covariate distance sampling, with which I am only vaguely familiar, t=
o=20
yield better adjusted values? Is there any way I can end up with better=20=

detection functions and therefore more reasonable probability of detectio=

n=20
estimates?

Thanks for reading my book. I look forward to any advice.

Matt

The easy way, assuming each point is entered as a sample in Distance, is=20=

to set up a new Model Definition and tick the box to estimate density by=20=

sample in the Estimate tab. If you want abundance by point, it's simply=20=

density*pi*w^2 where w is truncation distance.

However, if you want to calculate abundance in each sample (point) by=20
hand, you can use the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator: estimated=20
abundance =3D sum(1/estimated p_i) where the sum is over all animals coun=
ted=20
at the point, and p_i is the estimated probability of detecting the ith=20=

animal, given it is within the truncation distance. To calculate p_i, se=
e=20
the Distance online help -- look in the index under Detection function,=20=

formulae, about. Note that if you don't have animal level covariates=20
(which it appears you don't) then p_i will be the same for all animals at=
=20
a point, so the above reduces to estimated abundance =3D n/p where n i=
s=20
the count at the point and p is the estimated probability of detecting an=
=20
animal given it is within the truncation distance.

As an aside, assuming that your stands vary in size, then by locating one=
=20
point in each stand you have a design with a different proportion of the=20=

stand area surveyed in each point (different "coverage probability" in=20=

each stand). If you're also interested in calculating an average density=
=20
over all stands, you'll need to take this into account. You could=20
calculate a weighted mean of the stand densities, with the weight being=20=

the proportion of the stand area surveyed.

Hope this helps,

I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but=20=

=20
probability of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the=20
point and that the animal is present within the truncation distance. You=

then want to calculate density (or abundance) at each point using this=20=

habitat-specific probability of detection.

You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the Model=

to =96 but it's going to require some work. We want p_i, the probability=
of=20

=20
distance. Note, this isn't the probability of detecting the animal at=20=

it's observed distance -- it's the probability given that the animal was=20=

somewhere between 0 and w. We could use the observed distances but then=20=

m=20

to integrate this function between 0 and w, using numerical integration=20=

still

Cheers,

Hi Nick, list,

What you're proposing is what we sometimes call "spatial modeling"=20
or "spatial density surface estimation". I'll attempt an answer, but I'm=
=20
no expert so others may want to contribute more. Also, there's some stuf=
f=20
on this in Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.

To begin with, you need to do the detection function modeling in=20
Distance. You could either stratify by habitat, or put habitat in as a=20=

factor covariate in the MCDS engine. If you have enough data, and no=20
problems such as avoidance, rounding, etc, then you could try both and le=
t=20
AIC tell you which is better. If using MCDS then you could include other=
=20
covariates too. Once you've finished this modeling, you want an estimate=
=20
of detection probability by point (p_k) (Note, I'm omitting hats from=20
estimates to avoid cumbersome text notation. Also, for now, I'm assuming=
=20
you don't have any species level covariates such as cluster size). To do=
=20
this, you ask for density by sample, as in my reply to "Adjusting counts=
=20
for delectability and covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004).

Now you need to incorporate the estimates of p_k into the spatial model=20=

for the bird counts. To my knowledge there are three ways to do this:

1. Divide the observed count at each point n_k by the estimated p_k to ge=
t=20
an estimate of abundance at each point N_k. This abundance is non-
integer, so:

2. you might want to divide N_k by the area of each point (pi*w^2) to get=
=20
an estimated density at each point D_k. Doesn't make much difference=20
really. Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson error=20=

term as the response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?=20

3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use=20=

pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius for=20=

that point.

Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the=20
counts. However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level=20
covariates, such as sex of bird or cluster size. In that case, you don't=
=20
know what the effective detection radius is when you observe no birds --=20=

but you do know that the estimate of density is 0. If you have species=20=

level covariates in 1 or 2 you estimate N_k by the sum of 1/p_i for each=20=

bird i detected at the point. There is a section of the online manual=20=

that says how to calculate p_i for each animal given the parameter=20
estimates of the detection function.

In practice, two problems usually present themselves:

1. Overdispersion. Often many points have 0 birds seen, so you get data=20=

with lots of zeros and relatively few high counts (or high D_ks if the=20=

p_ks are sometimes small). Can be hard to model. Can perhaps investigat=
e=20
the various zero-inflated models that are out there?

2. Variance estimation. How does one incorporate the variance due to=20
estimating the detection function in the final variance estimate from the=
=20
spatial model? An easy way is a nonparametric bootstrap or jackknife of=20=

points, but you need plenty of points for this. Various parametric=20
bootstraps have been proposed - I think there is something on this in=20
Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book. It may be possible to=20=

do something analytic based on the delta method -- don't know.

So, hope this helps -- as I said others may be able to contribute more.=20=

Cheers,

Argh! Hopefully you can do your bit in training people to make=20
intelligent use of the program. Also, I've found in general that people=20=

who have a poor understanding of the program options also have a poor=20
understanding of how to design surveys and implement field methods that=20=

give reliable results. Just my prejudice I guess.

> >Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated

> >answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will=

> >suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
> >already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
> >My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
> >density estimate outright?

I'm afraid it's not that simple. Getting a reliable estimate requires=20=

more than just an "adequate" sample size of observations, and the require=
d=20
sample size depends on factors such as the type of survey (points require=
=20
more than lines), and shape of the detection function (wide shoulders=20
require fewer observations to accurately model). Also, remember that you=
=20
also need a "decent" sample size of lines or points for reliable=20
estimation of the encounter rate variance.

Here's a very rough checklist for initial assessment of a study:

- were the lines/points laid out according to a randomized survey design?=
=20=20
Ideally there should be 20 or more lines or points - many fewer than that=
=20
and I'd doubt the encounter rate variance estimates. If the analysis is=20=

stratified, you'd like 20 lines per stratum if possible.

- is g(0) likely to be 1?

- is animal movement likely to be a problem? (is there evasive movement,=20=

or do animals move at more than 1/3-half the speed of the observer for=20=

line transects; were the point transects performed over a "long" time=20
period (ie not a snapshot)

- were distances measured accurately?

- does the detection function have a wide shoulder?

- is the sample size of observations reasonable? (60-80 recommended,=20
although for wide shoulders and line transects can get away with far=20
fewer). If the detection function is estimated by stratum, you'd like 60-=

80 observations by stratum if possible.

- does the analysis look like it was performed competently?

- do the reported results give both the estimate and CI/CV, and=20
interpretation of the results take account of the uncertainty in the=20
estimate.

I've probably forgotten something, but hope this helps. Perhaps someone=20=

else will be willing to stick their neck out and offer more absolute rule=
s=20
of thumb!

- Len
